title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Urinary Tract Infection in Children From 8 Days to 5 Years of Age
summary: The 2026 AAP guideline expands UTI guidance to medically noncomplex children from 8 days through 5 years and uses GRADE methodology. It suggests antibiotic courses of 7 days or less for most children, with age- and syndrome-specific durations, and recommends oral rather than hospitalization-requiring parenteral or sequential therapy for children older than 28 days and younger than 5 years who tolerate oral treatment and do not otherwise require admission. It also updates post-UTI imaging, including renal/bladder ultrasonography after a first febrile UTI and a suggestion against routine VCUG when ultrasonography is normal.
findings: The guideline contains 8 Key Action Statements: 2 strong and 6 conditional recommendations, with certainty ranging from low to very low.
For most pediatric UTI, the panel suggests a shorter antibiotic course of 7 days or less rather than more than 7 days; suggested durations vary by age and clinical syndrome.

For children older than 28 days and younger than 5 years who tolerate oral therapy and do not otherwise need hospitalization, the panel recommends oral antibiotics rather than parenteral or sequential therapy requiring hospitalization.
After a first febrile UTI in children younger than 5 years, the guideline recommends renal/bladder ultrasonography and suggests against routine VCUG when ultrasonography is normal.
comparator: Prior AAP UTI guidance and the longer or more intensive management strategies addressed by individual recommendations.
population: Medically noncomplex infants and children 8 days through 5 years of age with suspected or diagnosed urinary tract infection.
shortTitle: AAP 2026: pediatric UTI diagnosis and treatment

corrections.description: Adjusted topic labels to supported site categories and corrected the publisher link to the retrieved canonical URL.

limitations: Most recommendations are conditional and supported by low- or very-low-certainty evidence. The guideline is intended for medically noncomplex children and does not replace separate higher-risk pathways for young febrile infants or children with major comorbidity.
intervention: Updated diagnostic, antibiotic-duration, route-of-therapy, imaging, and recurrence-prevention recommendations for pediatric UTI.
whyItMatters: For stable young children with UTI, this supports shorter antibiotic courses and less routine IV treatment or admission when oral therapy is feasible. It also gives ED clinicians a clearer framework for discharge imaging follow-up after a first febrile UTI.
evidenceNotes: Official AAP guideline page and publisher PDF reviewed. Catch-up: previously missed important publication. The publisher labels the article free to read but not Open Access.
primaryEndpoint: Eight Key Action Statements and four Good Practice Statements covering evaluation, treatment, imaging, and prevention.
guidelineStrength: Eight Key Action Statements: 2 strong and 6 conditional recommendations; supporting certainty is predominantly low to very low.
